name: Locus of control
aliases: Internal versus external control of reinforcement
statement: People differ in how far they believe outcomes follow from their own actions rather than from luck, fate or powerful others.
meaning: Rotter put the idea inside social learning theory. Whether a reward changes behaviour depends on whether the person reads the reward as contingent on what they did. The generalised expectancy about that contingency is what the scale measures. Someone at the internal end treats results as following from effort and skill. Someone at the external end treats them as following from chance, fate or people with power. Siraji and Haque describe Rotter's instrument as 23 scored item pairs in a forced-choice format plus six filler pairs, with totals running from 0 to 23 and higher totals meaning more external. Marsh and Richards report that Rotter concluded in 1966 and again in 1975 that responses to the scale were unidimensional, or at least that one general factor explained most of the variance in the total score. Both of those descriptions of Rotter come from later papers, because the monograph could not be obtained. The construct is a stable difference between people rather than an error anyone commits on a given occasion, which is why it sits awkwardly beside the judgement biases in this corpus.

origin.note: Pages 1 to 28 of volume 80, issue 1, introducing the I-E scale. Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all record the monograph as closed, and no repository copy was found, so it was not read for this entry and nothing is quoted from it.

evidence: The scale was built as one dimension, and the first challenges to that came within a decade. Hanna Levenson told the 1973 American Psychological Association convention that lumping fate, chance and powerful others together under one heading was the problem, and she split externality in two. Her I, P and C scales carry eight items each in a Likert format, presented to the respondent as a single 24-item attitude scale. She reports Kuder-Richardson reliabilities in the mid .60s and high .70s for a student group, Spearman-Brown split-half figures in the mid .60s for an adult sample, and one-week test-retest figures in the .60s and .70s. In a college sample of 75 the P and C scales correlated with Rotter externality at .25 and .56, and the I scale at -.41. Two principal component analyses, one on 329 college males and one on 165 psychiatric inpatients, produced I, P and C as the first three factors, together accounting for 60% of the total variance. Levenson also reports that the P and C scales correlate with each other between .23 and .59 and are usually unrelated to the I scale, which is not what a bipolar dimension predicts. Marsh and Richards reviewed 20 published factor analyses of Rotter's own scale and counted six distinguishable factors across them. Their confirmatory analysis found that a five-factor model fitted adequately while models with fewer factors or a simpler structure did not, and that a single higher-order factor still explained much of the variance in the lower-order factors. Beretvas and colleagues later ran a reliability generalisation study across published uses of Rotter's scale and of the Nowicki-Strickland scale. They found no statistically significant difference between the two scales in predicted internal consistency, and only the percentage of women in a sample predicted variation in internal consistency estimates. Testing interval length explained variation in the test-retest coefficients.

replication.headline: The correlates reproduce at modest size, around r = .30 for depression symptoms across 28,490 people, while the scale's single dimension and its separateness from neighbouring traits do not.
replication.detail: Cheng and colleagues pooled 152 independent samples covering 33,224 adults in 18 cultural regions. External locus of control correlated with depression symptoms at r = .30, 95% CI .27 to .32, across 123 samples and 28,490 people. Anxiety symptoms gave r = .30, 95% CI .27 to .33, across 65 samples and 13,208 people. Individualism explained 20% of unique variance in the anxiety link only: the correlation was .20, 95% CI .13 to .28, in 8 collectivist samples totalling 2,297 people, against .32, 95% CI .29 to .34, in 54 individualist samples totalling 9,887. The collectivist side of that contrast rests on those 8 samples. At work the answer depends on which correlation is quoted. Judge and Bono's meta-analysis, built on 274 correlations, gives estimated true score correlations of .32 between internal locus of control and job satisfaction and .22 with job performance. Wang, Bowling and Eschleman report mean observed correlations for general locus of control of .22 with global job satisfaction, 95% CI .17 to .26, across 44 samples and 12,197 people, and .07 with job performance, 95% CI .03 to .12, across 16 samples and 3,893 people. Their work-specific measure did better on both, at .34 and .16. Health behaviour is weaker still. Cheng, Cheung and Lo pooled 76 samples of 76,580 people on specific health behaviours and found average correlations with the three health locus of control dimensions running from -.07 to .10. For global health appraisal, across 95 samples and 12,068 people, the correlations ran from -.16 to .21, and all were statistically significant except the one between powerful others and mental quality of life. The structural claims fare worse than the correlational ones. Lange and Tiggemann factored the I-E scale in Australian students and report that it is not additive but multidimensional, with two largely independent factors covering personal and political control. On retest 8 of the 9 General Control items loaded again on the first factor and all 5 Political Control items on the second, and the scale's test-retest reliability was .61. Walkey gave the Rotter and Levenson scales to 71 male and 85 female students, confirmed Levenson's three factors and added further evidence that Rotter's scale is multidimensional. Siraji and Haque had to discard 11 of the 23 items before one factor would fit their Bangla translation in 300 adults, and the 12 retained items explained 32% of the variance. Callan and colleagues ran the 23-item scale on 429 analysed participants of 450 requested, under a preregistered plan, and report an alpha of 0.79 with a hierarchical omega of 0.47. Petrowski and colleagues gave the four-item IE-4 short scale to a German sample of 2,522 and conclude it is best treated as unifactorial once acquiescence is modelled as a separate method factor. The sharpest challenge is to the construct's separateness. Judge, Erez, Bono and Thoresen ran four studies on self-esteem, neuroticism, locus of control and generalised self-efficacy. They report that a single factor explained the relationships among measures of the four traits, that discriminant validity was relatively poor, and that each trait added little incremental variance in predicting external criteria beyond the higher order construct. Judge later put the average correlation among the four at .59, and noted that locus of control fits the core self-evaluations typology less well than the other three do. On cohort change, Twenge, Zhang and Im report a shift toward externality of about .80 standard deviations between 1960 and 2002, and say the average college student in 2002 was more external than 80% of college students in the early 1960s. Their data are 97 college samples of 18,310 students and 41 child samples of 6,554 children aged 9 to 14, with birth cohort and time period explaining 14% of the variance. Wang and Xin ran the same design on Chinese college students and found no significant change in Rotter scores between 2001 and 2019, and none in Levenson's internality, powerful others or chance scores between 1997 and 2018. Rudolph and colleagues put the cross-temporal method itself through a Monte Carlo study. With 25 studies of 200 people, a population standard deviation of 0.50 and the smallest simulated cohort effect, the method returned an estimate with a bias of 8.397 against the parameter; with 50 studies, a standard deviation of 1.50 and the largest simulated effect, the bias was 0.647. Within a person the construct moves little. Cobb-Clark and Schurer, using seven mastery items in the Australian HILDA panel, report a one-year correlation of 0.605 and a four-year correlation of 0.517. Over four years 25.0% of men and 27.5% of women shifted by more than one standard deviation.

study.cite: Cheng, C., Cheung, S. F., Chio, J. H., & Chan, M. S. (2013). Cultural meaning of perceived control: A meta-analysis of locus of control and psychological symptoms across 18 cultural regions. Psychological Bulletin, 139(1), 152-188.

limits: Locus of control is an individual-difference construct, not a judgement error, so the `state` vocabulary of this site is a poor fit for it. There is no single experimental effect to repeat. The resolution used here is to read `replication` as asking whether the measure's structure and its published correlates hold up when other people test them, which is the question the literature has in fact argued about. That reading yields `mixed`: the correlates reproduce at modest size across tens of thousands of people, and the unidimensional structure and the discriminant validity do not. The structural verdict needs one qualification. Marsh and Richards found strong evidence against unidimensionality and still found that a single higher-order factor fitted the data reasonably, which is why the total score is contested rather than empty. Several things could not be obtained. Rotter's 1966 monograph is recorded as closed by Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar, and no repository copy surfaced in searches of the Internet Archive, Temple University's digital library, PsycNet and general web search on 17 August 2026, so the reliabilities Rotter reported are absent here. His 1975 reply on misconceptions and his 1990 retrospective were also not opened. Ng, Sorensen and Eby's 2006 meta-analysis of locus of control at work is described from its Crossref abstract, which carries no figures; Wiley and JSTOR returned HTTP 403 for the full text, and the workplace numbers here come from Wang, Bowling and Eschleman instead. Judge, Erez, Bono and Thoresen's 2002 paper was read at its PubMed abstract, and the .59 is quoted from Judge's own 2009 review of it rather than from the 2002 paper. Marsh and Richards is quoted from its PubMed abstract. Beretvas and colleagues' paper is described from its Crossref abstract, so the average reliability it estimates is not quoted. Levenson's peer-reviewed 1973 paper in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology has no abstract on PubMed and was not opened; the Levenson figures here come from her 1973 convention paper, which ERIC hosts in full. Cobb-Clark and Schurer's figures come from the 2011 IZA working paper; the 2013 Economic Journal version is closed and was not read, and their measure is the Pearlin and Schooler mastery items rather than Rotter's scale. Presson and Benassi's 1996 meta-analysis of locus of control and depressive symptoms was sought at Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and general web search, has no Crossref record, and nothing from it appears here.
misreadings: The most common is that internal is good and external is bad. Cheng and colleagues found the external locus of control to anxiety link half as strong in collectivist societies as in individualist ones, and wrote that external locus of control does not carry the same negative connotations across cultures. The second is treating an I-E total as one number. Lange and Tiggemann report the scale is not additive but multidimensional, Marsh and Richards count six factors across 20 published analyses, and Callan and colleagues put the hierarchical omega of the 23-item total at 0.47. The third is treating locus of control as a trait of its own in a list beside self-esteem and neuroticism. Judge, Erez, Bono and Thoresen found a single factor behind all four and poor discriminant validity among them. The fourth concerns the cohort claim. Twenge's .80 standard deviation shift is quoted as a fact about young people everywhere. The same design run on Chinese students by Wang and Xin found no significant change over two decades, and Rudolph and colleagues show the method over- and under-estimates cohort effects depending on the conditions. The fifth is a conflation: health locus of control, measured on Wallston's three dimensions, is a domain-specific descendant of Rotter's general scale rather than the same instrument, and its links to specific health behaviours sit between -.07 and .10. The sixth is reading a workplace correlation without asking which kind it is. Judge and Bono's .32 for job satisfaction is an estimated true score correlation; Wang, Bowling and Eschleman's mean observed correlation for the same general measure is .22.
